unit.title: Example: internal model tracks RPV over a 2.5-year period

claim.text: The source describes the speaker's internal model: it calculates RPV for all brands during the order process and looks at revenue per visitor over a 2 and 1/2 year time period to understand if it is going up or down, which tells whether conversion rate is improving or getting worse; they do not look at conversion rate.
claim.quote: In fact, in our internal model, how we calculate this for all brands during the order process. So, we look at revenue per visitor over a 2 and 1/2 year time period to get an understanding if this is going up or going down and that tells us whether conversion rate is improving or getting worse. We don't look at conversion rate.

unknowns: This describes the speaker's internal model; the source does not establish 2 and 1/2 years as a general recommendation or required tracking period.

unit.title: Example: low-AOV impulse store relied on Google because Meta could not work

claim.text: The source describes a real store with a 9% conversion rate and low average order value around $45 to $55; it was an impulse purchase with most traffic from bottom-of-funnel Google, and because the average order value was that low, Meta could not work, so the only paid platform that would work was Google. This is presented as one historical store example, not a general platform-selection rule.
claim.quote: store number one, 9% conversion rate, but a low average order value around about $45 to $55. It's an impulse purchase and majority of the traffic is coming from bottom of funnel on Google because with an average order value that low, you just can't get meta to work. So, the only platform that's going to work for paid is going to be Google.

unknowns: The source presents this as one real store example; the approximately $45 to $55 AOV is not established as a general threshold for excluding Meta or selecting Google.

reasons: The action, sequencing, and qualification that UI should reinforce measurement, messaging, and consumer psychology are directly stated in the excerpt.
The exclusion is appropriately limited to relying on small UI changes as CRO, rather than excluding UI altogether.
The excerpt explicitly characterizes conversion rate as not directly pullable and as an output of about 50 inputs, most outside the page.
The candidate preserves the source's uncertainty by noting that the inputs are not enumerated.
The excerpt explicitly identifies RPV as the better metric and gives the stated calculation: conversion rate multiplied by average order value.
The excerpt describes contribution per visitor as the profit-contribution-oriented version of the metric, obtained by additionally applying gross-margin percentage.
It also expressly advises against incorporating CAC and advertising expenses in this metric and instead keeping it simple as gross profit per visitor.
The excerpt reports that the speaker's internal model looks at RPV over 2.5 years; it does not establish 2.5 years as a general recommendation or necessary tracking period.
The candidate should distinguish this described internal practice from a prescriptive action for all users.
The excerpt explicitly says that conversion rate should be replaced by RPV for decision-making because RPV is directly tied to revenue per visitor.

The candidate retains the source's qualifiers: page quality does not often set the ceiling, and another design test is usually not the next lever only after clarity, offer, and proof have been taken as far as they can go.
It accurately identifies the alternative levers named in the excerpt, including first-order contribution margin, launches, product quality, and repeat purchasing.
The excerpt specifically criticizes repeatedly redesigning the same page to seek a new ceiling when slight page-design changes were not the constraint.
The excerpt expressly qualifies its critique of conversion rate by saying that brands should still undertake substantial landing-page optimization and get conversion rates as high as possible.
The source states that ongoing slight tweaks generally do not materially move RPV and says that at 'like 40 million plus online' A/B testing begins to be worthwhile for roughly an additional 0.1%.
The candidate preserves the approximate nature of the threshold and the source's qualification that this is not worthwhile for most people.
The direct calculation in the action, ad spend divided by new-customer orders, is explicitly provided in the excerpt.
The candidate also retains the source's caveat that new-customer sessions and new-customer conversion rate are hard to delineate.
The excerpt makes this exact conditional CAC argument: conversion rate is in the denominator, a doubling would halve CAC, and restoring the CAC ceiling could allow substantially more volume.
The candidate includes the material limitation that doubling conversion rate is described as an extreme result the speaker has almost never seen achieved.

The source directly contrasts conversion-rate improvement with greater ad spend and platform-efficiency work, stating that the latter generally require money while conversion-rate improvement need not.
The candidate does not invent specific landing-page tactics that the excerpt does not enumerate.
The excerpt describes one historical store example; it does not establish a generally applicable platform-selection rule for all low-AOV impulse-purchase stores.
The approximately $45–$55 AOV is an attribute of that example, not a supported threshold for excluding Meta or selecting Google.

The trigger also includes that most traffic is already coming from bottom-of-funnel Google, so using that condition to prescribe Google is circular rather than demonstrating a platform-choice dependency.

Although the excerpt says, "This retailer would get massive gains by being able to go to 1.1%," the preceding comparison identifies brand B as having a 1% conversion rate. The statement can therefore naturally refer to brand B moving from 1% to 1.1%.
The candidate incorrectly frames the statement as an inconsistency with the earlier 9% store and invents a conflict with the Google-store candidate.
It should retain the ambiguous referent if necessary, rather than assert that the 1.1% figure is a typo or a target for the 9% store.

The full excerpt explicitly says not to conclude that a friend's brand, competitor, or agency client is better merely because it has a higher conversion rate, since conversion rate reflects many underlying variables.

omissions.description: The candidates do not represent the source's advice that conversion rate will generally decline as acquisition is scaled into colder traffic, which is a material reason not to compare conversion rates across brands or traffic mixes.
omissions.quote: And one of them is volume on cold traffic. And the more you scale into cold, the lower conversion rate will generally become.

source_limitations: The excerpt ends mid-sentence at "Now another argument for why conversion rate is", so later qualifications or recommendations are unavailable.
Several statements are presented as the speaker's assertions or historical examples without underlying data, methodology, or independently verifiable evidence in the excerpt.
The transcript contains ambiguous or malformed wording, including "blue sense orientated" and "Microsoft CAC," which limits confidence in the exact intended meaning of those passages.
The referent of "This retailer would get massive gains by being able to go to 1.1%" is not explicitly named, though the immediately preceding discussion of the 1% brand provides a plausible referent.
